title: Remembering the dead

lines: A CABINET IN THE LIVING ROOM.
cards: A wooden cabinet stands in the corner of a living room in Japan. Behind small doors there's an image of the Buddha, a bell, a little bowl of rice, and thin lacquered tablets with names written on them.
Each morning someone opens the doors, lights incense, rings the bell, and sets out fresh rice and tea. The names belong to grandparents and great-grandparents.
They're only ink on wood, but they're greeted every morning anyway. A funeral happens once. What comes after can go on for years.

teach.b: Buddhist families keep the dead close in two ways: an altar at home and a day in the year.

teach.h: NEAR THE BUDDHA, NOT AS GODS.
teach.b: In Japan it's called a butsudan, a Buddha cabinet, and the names of the family's dead are kept beside the Buddha. In Chinese and Vietnamese homes, ancestor tablets sit on a family altar. The pairing matters.
The dead aren't worshipped as gods. They're placed near the Buddha, and offerings are made in the presence of the teaching. Then the day.
East Asia has a yearly festival for the dead, called Obon in Japan, which you met earlier on the path, and Yulan or the Ghost Festival in China. Its story comes from the Ullambana Sutra.
A disciple of the Buddha, Maudgalyayana, known in the texts for his powers, looks for his dead mother and finds her reborn as a hungry ghost, starving.
He offers her a bowl of rice, and it bursts into flame before it reaches her mouth. He runs to the Buddha, who tells him his own power isn't enough.
At the end of the rainy-season retreat, he should make offerings to the whole community of monks, for his mother and his ancestors. He does, and in the story his mother is freed.
So the yearly rite isn't one person's effort. It's a family, a community, a whole season of practice, pointed at the ones who came before.
In Japan, Obon is kept with lanterns and dances that welcome the dead home, then send them off again.
Remembering the dead is something done together.

how: Buddhist families in many countries keep a home altar with the names or photographs of their dead beside an image of the Buddha, offering incense, food and light; in East Asia the yearly Obon or Ghost Festival honors ancestors with offerings to the monastic community, lanterns and gatherings.

o: worshipping ancestors as gods who answer prayers
a home altar and a yearly rite that keep the dead close
a single ceremony held on the day of the burial

games.q: you're Maudgalyayana. your mother is a hungry ghost and the rice you offer bursts into flame. what does the Buddha tell you?
o: try harder with your own powers.
make offerings to the whole community of monks.
accept that nothing can be done.
games.why: at the end of the rains retreat, he gives to the whole community for his mother's sake, and in the story she is freed.

practice: If you have a candle or a small lamp, light it carefully, and bring to mind someone who has died, maybe yesterday's person, maybe someone else, saying their name silently or out loud.

Let the small flame keep them company while you breathe; you don't need to say or feel anything in particular. If the loss feels too heavy to carry alone, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

wordCard.voice: Remembering the dead. A home altar where the names sit near the Buddha, and a yearly rite where a whole community gives in their name. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali peta (Sanskrit preta): one who has departed; also the hungry ghost Maudgalyayana's mother became.

carryVoice: Your line: they are remembered. A name said aloud is one way the dead stay close. Rest well.
